https://www.dw.com/en/alleged-irish-crim.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IWrf Kinahan was extradited to Ireland from the UAE Image: Mark Marlow/PA Images/picture alliance Advertisement Suspected international crime boss Daniel Kinahan landed in Ireland on Sunday after being extradited from the United Arab Emirates . Following his arrival in Ireland, prosecutors charged Kinahan with directing a criminal organization during a special court sitting. Kinahan, 49, was arrested in April in Dubai after Ireland issued a warrant for "alleged serious organized crime offenses." He is accused of being the leader of a cartel linked to drug smuggling and money laundering. Irish authorities deployed an enhanced security convoy to escort the supsected crime ringleader to court Image: Brian Lawless/PA Images/picture alliance What do we know about the allegations against Kinahan? The group is thought to be the most powerful criminal organization in Ireland, with Irish police estimating its wealth at more than €1 billion ($1.15 billion). The alleged crime boss had lived openly in the UAE for about a decade before his arrest. He moved there from Spain around 2016 after the murder of one of his associates and an attempt on his life. In 2022, the United States imposed sanctions on Kinahan after linking his organization to some of the world's most notorious crime networks and offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest. The group is linked to a brutal feud with a smaller Irish syndicate that has resulted in 18 murders. “Since February 2016, the (Kinahan Organized Crime Group) has been involved in a gang war with another group in Ireland and Spain, resulting in numerous murders, including of two innocent bystanders,” the US Treasury Department said. Kinahan is the second alleged senior member of the cartel to be extradited to Ireland from Dubai. Sean McGovern was extradited in 2024 and was ultimately sentenced to 24 years in prison after pleading guilty to directing organized crime and attempted murder. Irish media reported that a special security convoy would be deployed to escort Kinahan to the Special Criminal Court, which handles offenses related to terrorism and organized crime. UAE, Ireland hail judicial cooperation in Kinahan extradition In a joint statement, the justice minister of the UAE and Ireland called Kinahan "one of the most high-profile individuals sought for prosecution in connection with transnational organized crime." Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan called the extradition a "landmark of judicial cooperation with Dubai," adding that it "sends a clear message that suspected perpetrators of serious and organized crime will find no safe haven from justice." Meanwhile, Foreign Minister Helen McEntee hailed the outcome as "the culmination of years of determined work" by Irish authorities under various governments. https://www.dw.com/en/norway-seizes-russ.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5L0dJ The research vessel was taking a group of researchers to Barentsburg, a Russian coal mining settlement on the Arctic Svalbard archipelago Image: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance Advertisement Norwegian courts have ordered the seizure of a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce part of a $4.22 billion (roughly €3.6 billion) compensation claim won by Ukrainian state energy firm Naftogaz after Moscow's seizure of its assets in Crimea , which Russia illegally annexed in 2014. Officials announced that the ship had been stopped from departing the port in the Russian coal mining settlement of Barentsburg in the Svalbard archipelago late on Wednesday. Svalbard has been Norwegian territory since 1925 but is a demilitarized zone where people from dozens of countries, Russia included, can settle without visas under certain conditions. Russia's ambassador to Norway said that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels. Around two thirds of Svalbard is designated as national parks and nature reserves, but the coal mining settlement of Barentsburg is home to about a tenth of the archipelago's population Image: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance What do we know about the Professor Molchanov ship being impounded? The first group to announce the ship's seizure was Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz as it tries to secure the compensation awarded to it by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague in 2023. Russia had refused to pay the fine plus legal fees and interest amid its ongoing war with Ukraine , and Naftogaz has since begun trying to secure the seizure and forced sale of Russian commercial assets via local courts instead. "Russia cannot evade ​responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," said Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko. Covington said it had been tracking the ship, the Professor Molchanov , for months. It said its application was approved on Monday by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court, which ordered Svalbard's governor to ensure the ship stayed in dock once it arrived. The end of coal mining in Svalbard To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The Svalbard governor's office later issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held in Svalbard. "The governor will take care of the crew and passengers on board the vessel in collaboration with Trust Arktikugol," it said, referring to the Russian enterprise (meaning "Arctic Coal") that administers the Barentsburg mining settlement. Norway's Justice Ministry, meanwhile, said the issue did not directly concern the government in Oslo. "Russia can demand that ​the district court reassess the case," the Justice ‌Ministry said. How did Russia respond? Russia's ambassador to Norway, Nikolai Korchunov, said in a statement on Thursday that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels. "We insist on the immediate release of the vessel and on ensuring the safety of its passengers and crew," he said. The Kremlin also summoned Norway's ambassador in Moscow to lodge a formal complaint. Is Svalbard Russia's real leverage in the Arctic? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The Professor Molchanov , a repurposed research vessel, arrived in Barentsburg on Tuesday with a party of Russian scientists, according to a journalist who was accompanying them. "The seizure has had no impact on the expedition participants or the ship's crew. No one has been arrested. We are all going about our business as usual," Andrei Gorbunov, editor-in-chief of Komsomolskaya Pravda (KP) radio wrote on KP's website. He said that for the time being, "the Professor Molchanov is simply forbidden from leaving the port of Barentsburg," adding it was unclear how long this would remain the case. Prior to the war in Ukraine Barentsburg was also home to Ukrainian and other foreign nationals. But most have since left, Ukrainians in particular were told to accept an offer of Russian citizenship or leave. Image: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance What is behind Svalbard's special status, and why is it home to the Barentsburg settlement? Svalbard is an archipelago well to the north of mainland Norway in the Arctic Circle, sparsely populated and thought to be home to slightly fewer than 3,000 people. It was a whaling base in the 17th and 18th centuries and became a coal mining site at the beginning of the 20th century. The territory was recognized as part of Norway in 1925, but only after the 1920 establishment of an international treaty — which nowadays has dozens of signatories — designating the area a demilitarized zone where anybody from a signatory state was permitted to settle and work without a visa , provided they met certain conditions. The Soviet Union eventually acquired three sites and developed them as company towns: Barentsburg, with a remnant population of around 300 mostly Russian nationals, the nearly-abandoned settlement of Pyramiden, and Grumant, which has been left as a ghost town for decades. Tourism has become a growth industry on the stark but stunning polar archipelago. https://www.dw.com/en/us-confirms-it-has.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MbSY The Space Force, a relatively new branch of the US military, was created by US President Donald Trump in 2019 Image: Cover-Images/IMAGO Advertisement The United States has weapons deployed in spatial orbit, the US Space Force announced, confirming the existence of such capabilities for the first time. "The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," a US Space Force spokesperson said in a press release. The statement did not provide specifics on the weapons in question. "Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain — employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities," it said, adding that "these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes." US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink also confirmed the existence of US weapons in space, while speaking at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Monday. The Space Force, the US military's arm dedicated to space, justified the weapons deployment by citing its two biggest geopolitical rivals — Russia and China . It said both countries pose a threat to American interests in space. China "develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernization strategy," while Russia "views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts," the statement read. AI and satellites: The new nuclear watchdogs? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What have China and Russia said? In response, China urged Washington to "stop preparing for war" in outer space. "We urge the US side to stop expanding its military capabilities and preparing for war in outer space," Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said, warning against an "arms race" in space. Russia on Tuesday also called for space to be kept free of weapons. "We believe that space must be free of any weapon," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow , adding: "We are counting on broad international consolidation to continue working toward the complete demilitarization of space." The final frontier The militarization of space is an issue as old as the race to space itself. In 1967, the world's biggest superpowers and other nations signed the Outer Space Treaty addressing the single biggest concern — the deployment of nuclear weapons in space. Since then, Russia, the US, India and China have been exploring ways to fight in space outside of that treaty. That includes targeting each other's satellites critical for military communication, navigation and surveillance. Will Elon Musk give Ukraine Starlink's eyes over Russia? https://www.clarksvilleonline.com/2026/1.text: News Arts/Leisure Business Education Events Opinion Commentary Politics Spirituality Tech/Science Sports Home News Arts/Leisure Business Education Events Opinion Commentary Politics Spirituality Tech/Science Sports Home Education APSU Professor Dr. John Steinberg Named Visiting Professor at West Point Education APSU Professor Dr. John Steinberg Named Visiting Professor at West Point By News Staff Wednesday, October 14, 2026 Facebook X Pinterest Email Print Austin Peay State University Dr. John W. Steinberg’s West Point headshot. (Contributed photo) Clarksville, TN – Dr. John W. Steinberg, a professor of history and philosophy at Austin Peay State University (APSU), is spending the year teaching cadets at the United States Military Academy at West Point as the Charles Boal Ewing Chair in Military History. Steinberg, one of the world’s leading authorities on 19th- and 20th-century Russian military history, is serving in the role from July 1st, 2026, through May 31st, 2027. His path to West Point began with a simple request: library access for a book he was working on. “I was explaining this to [Dr. Greta Bucher], with whom I went to graduate school at Ohio State University in the 1980s, and who is the Russian historian at West Point,” Steinberg said. “I said, ‘Greta, can you set it up so I gain access to your military studies library for a couple of months?’ The next thing I knew, I got a call from the deputy chair of the Department of History and War Studies at West Point asking me if I was interested in applying to the position.” At West Point, Steinberg uses his knowledge of military history to train cadets and future officers for the U.S. Army. He applies lessons from history to decision-making models, creating a framework that these students will use in the field after they are commissioned as officers in the U.S. Army. “We don’t teach them that history repeats itself; we teach them [that] history offers lessons that might be used on that day when they have to decide who’s going to live and who’s going to die,” he said. Steinberg’s West Point experience has introduced him to a new learning environment and new types of students, but his Austin Peay State University background has prepared him well for the role. “I like teaching in any environment,” he said. “You always look for that sweet spot, which is where you sense that you’ve reached the edge of the student’s knowledge, and then you push. I did it at Austin Peay State University, I’ve done it elsewhere, and I’m doing it here.” Although he has not had much time to work on his book since his arrival at West Point, Steinberg has gained valuable research and teaching experience, which he hopes to bring back to Austin Peay. “My research has always focused on the education and training of Russian military elites,” he said. “So, the longer I’ve been a historian, the more of a comparison I have made on the way military leaders are educated and trained. We don’t think about this often enough, but military officers are some very smart people … I just have tremendous respect for what they’re trying to do. So, this deepens my knowledge, and it adds to the nuance of my research and conclusions.” Steinberg also anticipates that his West Point experience will make him a better guide on the annual study-abroad trip to Poland that he has led at Austin Peay for the past decade. This two-week journey allows students to visit several museums and historic sites in Krakow, Zamosc, Lublin and Warsaw while learning about Polish culture along the way. “They took us on a staff ride of the Battle of Gettysburg, and they were taking us spot by spot of where important encounters happened in that battle,” he said. “The tricks I learned and the things that I did that day will forever have a direct impact on the tours that I give in Poland.” Through his time as a visiting professor, Steinberg hopes to return to his roots in Russian military history and bring that focus back to Austin Peay State University. “I’ve always sought to return to my roots as a military historian … and in a left-handed kind of way, this opportunity presented itself,” he said. “So, I’m going to bring back my expertise that will be more finely tuned as a result of this experience, and the Austin Peay students will benefit from that.” Students interested in joining Dr. Steinberg on the history study-abroad program to Poland this summer can contact Dr. Dan Shea at shead@apsu.edu or visit the APSU study abroad program page. https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/fort.text: Forţele Aeriene ale SUA au declarat că au intervenit vineri seară în urma „unei activităţi suspecte a unor drone neautorizate” deasupra bazei RAF Lakenheath din Suffolk, Marea Britanie, relatează News.ro. Niciun membru al personalului, nicio aeronavă şi nicio infrastructură nu au fost afectate, a declarat un purtător de cuvânt al Forţelor Aeriene ale SUA. Această declaraţie vine în urma unor informaţii neconfirmate potrivit cărora la bază s-au declanşat sirenele, pe care locuitorii dintr-un sat din apropiere au declarat că le-au auzit. Ministerul Apărării a fost contactat pentru a oferi un comentariu, precizează BBC. La începutul acestei săptămâni, cel puţin 12 aeronave ale Forţelor Aeriene ale SUA au decolat de la baza RAF Mildenhall din apropiere. Urmărește știrile Digi24.ro și pe Google News
